Subject: SLA details: streaming vs non-streaming endpoints

Hi Marissa —

Thanks again for the demo last week. As we move toward procurement, procurement/legal have asked for clearer SLA language around the streaming endpoints versus the standard non-streaming REST endpoints. A few specific asks from our side: 

- Time-to-first-token (TTFT) expectations for streaming vs non-streaming (p50/p95/p99).
- Sustained tokens/sec expectations (per-connection and per-VM) and how you measure them.
- What counts as an exception (rolling upgrades, model switches, capacity failover) and whether credits apply differently for streaming vs sync endpoints.
- Any limits or fair-use rules that would allow Redwood to throttle or deny requests under normal operation.

Our target availability bar is 99.95% for the API overall, but we want to understand whether streaming endpoints will have different latency/service guarantees. Also, if there are known scenarios (e.g., heavy KV-cache warmup on very long contexts) that materially affect TTFT for streaming, please call them out.

Can you send a short write-up that we can use as a redline to the SOW? Happy to set up a call if it’s easier.

Thanks,

From: Rishi Malhotra <rishi_malhotra@redwood.ai>

Subject: RE: SLA details: streaming vs non-streaming endpoints — proposed metrics and measurement notes

Marissa/Vivek/Alicia —

I put together an engineering-first draft of how we measure and what we can commit to. High level: measurement must be precise about workload (prompt size, model family, sequence length, network RTT, and whether KV cache/prefix cache is warm). Below are baseline proposals; we can tighten for Dedicated or Private deployments where we control capacity.

Measurement conventions (important):
- TTFT (time-to-first-token): measured from request reception at the ingress (post TLS termination) to client-visible first byte. Measurement is averaged across successful requests. For streaming, TTFT is measured for the first chunk/frame delivered.
- Tokens/sec (throughput): measured as sustained token emission rate after the first 200ms warmup period; reported per-connection and per-node using a 60s rolling window.
- Percentiles: we report p50/p95/p99 for both TTFT and tokens/sec observed over the calendar month for the customer’s production traffic (sampled).

Baseline target commitments (Hosted API, mixed workloads, default model family):
- Non-streaming endpoints (sync generation): TTFT p50 = 140ms, p95 = 420ms, p99 = 900ms. Sustained throughput: 120–300 tokens/sec per connection depending on model and quantization.
- Streaming endpoints: TTFT p50 = 110ms, p95 = 360ms, p99 = 800ms (streaming sometimes improves perceived TTFT because we flush initial frames faster). Sustained tokens/sec: 200–700 tokens/sec per connection depending on model size and hardware; per-node aggregate throughput depends on instance type and batching policy.

Notes and constraints:
- Dedicated capacity: we can commit tighter numbers (reduce p95 by ~20–40%) once we validate model and instance type in staging.
- Private/on-prem: SLAs are measured differently; for air-gapped installs we provide operational targets and runbooks, but contractual financial credits are only available for Redwood-managed control plane options.
- Exceptions: rolling upgrades, model hot-swaps, and region-level outages are classified as permitted maintenance windows if we notify within the agreed window; however, prolonged degradation outside of maintenance is eligible for credits.

Suggested credit calculation (draft): monthly uptime shortfall and latency shortfall scaled by severity buckets; distinct buckets for streaming vs sync where degradation impacts business-critical streaming features (e.g., live transcripts). I will draft a concrete formula for the memo.

Happy to tighten any number if legal/procurement need more conservative guarantees.

Rishi
Principal Engineer, Serving Runtime

Subject: RE: SLA details: streaming vs non-streaming endpoints — contractual notes and exceptions process

A few product/contract notes to make this contract-ready: 

- Measurement windows: TTFT and tokens/sec percentiles should be computed monthly; we’ll publish a monthly report to the customer’s shared drive and surface anomalies in the Console.
- Exception handling:
  * Planned maintenance: 72-hour prior notice; maintenance windows don’t count against uptime SLO if scheduled and limited to the stated window.
  * Rolling model rollouts & kernel upgrades: may cause transient TTFT increases for streaming; these are considered "operational rollouts" and are covered under a lower SLA tier unless a rollback is requested.
  * Emergency scaling events (capacity exhaustion): if degradation is due to customer's traffic spikes exceeding committed throughput for Dedicated, we will first attempt autoscale/burst; if additional capacity is required and not provisioned within the committed timeframe, credits may apply.
- Fair use & throttling: we will define rate limits per route and per API key in the SOW attachment. Throttling only applies when consumption crosses defined thresholds; throttling behavior (HTTP 429 vs queuing) will be documented per endpoint type.
- Contract language for streaming: propose a one-paragraph exception that clarifies "streaming endpoints' TTFT and tokens/sec measurements exclude the first 5 seconds of a cold-started long-context generation for models >16K tokens and exclude client-side network delays." This prevents disputes where a user app adds large client-side delays.

Action items: Marissa to send an initial redline to Alicia with the attached SLA draft. Rishi to provide the concrete credit formula and measurement script so legal can validate. I’ll prepare SLO language suitable for inclusion in the SOW.

Vivek
Head of Product Operations
Redwood Inference
